def: The small cartilaginous tip at the lower end of the sternum, which ossifies with age. It is a landmark for CPR hand positioning and the T9 level.
The tough outer ring of fibrocartilage of an intervertebral disc, surrounding the gelatinous nucleus pulposus. Tears allow disc herniation.
A family of regulatory proteins that bind phosphorylated targets. Elevated 14-3-3 in cerebrospinal fluid supports a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Excess secretion of one or more pituitary hormones, usually from a pituitary adenoma, such as growth hormone (acromegaly) or prolactin.
Inflammation of the iris, causing a painful red eye, photophobia and a small irregular pupil. Anterior uveitis, associated with HLA-B27 diseases.
Inflammation of the choroid and retina at the back of the eye, causing floaters and vision loss. Seen in toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis and sarcoidosis.
Inflammation of the choroid, the vascular layer behind the retina, usually with retinal involvement (chorioretinitis).
The thin layer between the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium. Drusen deposits beneath it occur in macular degeneration, and breaks permit choroidal neovascularization.
Growth of abnormal new vessels from the choroid through Bruch membrane, causing wet age-related macular degeneration. Treated with anti-VEGF injections.
Growth of fragile new retinal vessels driven by ischemia and VEGF, as in proliferative diabetic retinopathy. They bleed into the vitreous.
A tear or hole in the retina that can let fluid under it and cause retinal detachment.
Severe, progressive nearsightedness with an elongated eye, causing retinal thinning, degeneration and risk of detachment.
Separation of the vitreous gel from the retina with aging, causing floaters and flashes. A tear in the retina may occur.
A fixed false belief of being infested with insects or parasites, often with skin picking; a delusional disorder, somatic type.
A delusion transferred from one person to a close partner, also called folie a deux.
Membrane channels that allow chloride ions to cross. CFTR is a chloride channel mutated in cystic fibrosis; GABA-A receptors are chloride channels.
Chemical modification of drugs in the body, mainly in the liver, in phase I (oxidation by CYP450) and phase II (conjugation) reactions.
Receptors for orexin (hypocretin), a hypothalamic neuropeptide that promotes wakefulness. Loss of orexin neurons causes narcolepsy type 1; suvorexant blocks the receptors.
Drugs that block the CYP3A4 enzyme, raising levels of its substrates. Examples are ketoconazole, macrolides, ritonavir and grapefruit juice.
A short-acting barbiturate that enhances GABA-A receptor chloride channel opening, used as a sedative.
A short-acting barbiturate that prolongs GABA-A chloride channel opening, used for sedation, refractory seizures and euthanasia.
An alpha-2 agonist sedative used in intensive care and procedures with little respiratory depression. Can cause bradycardia and hypotension.
Staphylococcus aureus toxins that cleave desmoglein-1, causing blistering of the superficial epidermis, as in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
A painful boil, an abscess of a hair follicle, usually from Staphylococcus aureus. Multiple recurrent furuncles are furunculosis.
A cluster of connected furuncles forming a deep abscess draining at multiple sites, usually from Staphylococcus aureus.
A volatile inhaled anesthetic with low blood solubility and rapid onset and recovery. Can irritate the airway.
An ester-type local anesthetic with long action, used in spinal and topical eye anesthesia.
An amide-type local anesthetic of intermediate duration, a sodium channel blocker.
An amide local anesthetic whose metabolite can cause methemoglobinemia, especially in newborns.
Short-term use of a rapidly acting anticoagulant (heparin) while warfarin is stopped before a procedure and its effect has worn off.
Excessive preoccupation with having a serious illness despite reassurance and few or no symptoms; now illness anxiety disorder.
False pregnancy: a woman believes she is pregnant and develops signs like amenorrhea and abdominal enlargement without a fetus.
An SSRI used mainly for obsessive-compulsive disorder. Inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP2C19.
An SNRI, the active metabolite of venlafaxine, used for depression.
An SNRI used for major depression.
A tricyclic-like antidepressant, a metabolite of loxapine, with dopamine-blocking effects that can cause extrapyramidal symptoms.
A tricyclic antidepressant with strong antihistamine effect; low doses are used for insomnia. Causes anticholinergic side effects.
A nonselective, irreversible MAO inhibitor for depression. Risks include hypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich foods and serotonin syndrome.
A nonselective irreversible MAO inhibitor for depression, with risk of hypertensive crisis with tyramine-rich foods.
A liver enzyme metabolizing caffeine, theophylline and clozapine. Induced by smoking and inhibited by ciprofloxacin and fluvoxamine.
A cluster A disorder with odd beliefs, magical thinking, eccentric behavior and social discomfort, without full psychosis.
A form of cognitive behavioral therapy combining acceptance and change skills, used mainly for borderline personality disorder and self-harm.
The hypothalamic area containing the hunger center and orexin neurons. Lesions cause anorexia and weight loss.
An enzyme that methylates and inactivates catecholamines and levodopa. Inhibitors (entacapone) extend levodopa's effect.
A dopamine metabolite formed by MAO and aldehyde dehydrogenase, further converted by COMT to homovanillic acid.
The ergot alkaloid core structure from which LSD is synthesized.
A hallucinogen acting as a serotonin 5-HT2A agonist, causing visual distortions and synesthesia, with flashbacks possible.
G-protein-coupled receptors CB1 (brain) and CB2 (immune cells) that mediate THC's effects.
A drug that decreases glutamate release, used in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to modestly prolong survival.
A long-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker that competitively blocks nicotinic receptors. Causes tachycardia by vagolytic effect.
A drug that reverses rocuronium and vecuronium by encapsulating and binding the neuromuscular blocker.
A tachykinin neuropeptide related to substance P, acting on NK2 receptors to cause bronchoconstriction and smooth muscle contraction.
Migraine drugs that block the receptor for calcitonin gene-related peptide, a vasodilating neuropeptide (the 'gepants').
The receptor for calcitonin gene-related peptide, a vasodilator neuropeptide released by trigeminal nerves in migraine.
Bacterial resistance from altered cell wall precursors (D-ala-D-lac in place of D-ala-D-ala), seen in enterococci (VRE) and rarely S. aureus.
A family (ABCC) of ATP-driven membrane pumps that move drugs and conjugated compounds out of cells, causing chemotherapy resistance.
The canalicular transporter that excretes conjugated bilirubin into bile. Defective in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
An MHC class I allele associated with hemochromatosis.
A dye that stains acidic structures like nuclei and ribosomes blue-purple; counterpart to eosin in H&E staining.
Free-radical oxidative damage of membrane lipids, forming reactive aldehydes. A mechanism of cell injury, as in carbon tetrachloride toxicity.
The basement membrane of the corneal endothelium, deep in the cornea. Copper deposits here form Kayser-Fleischer rings.
A radioactive element. Thorium dioxide was used as a contrast agent (Thorotrast) and is linked to liver angiosarcoma.
A radioactive contrast agent (Thorotrast) formerly used for imaging, causing hepatic angiosarcoma years later.
Seizures that persist despite adequate trials of two antiseizure medications. May be treated with surgery, vagus nerve stimulation or diet.
A mold that produces aflatoxin, a toxin on stored grains and peanuts that causes hepatocellular carcinoma.
Cells at the base of small intestinal crypts that secrete lysozyme and defensins for innate defense.
Duodenal compression between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta after weight loss, causing vomiting and postprandial pain.
Tiny channels between adjacent hepatocytes that collect bile and drain to bile ductules.
Vitamin A toxicity causing headache, pseudotumor cerebri, liver damage and bone pain, and birth defects in pregnancy.
The dome of the stomach above the esophageal opening. Gastroesophageal reflux can occur here; it is mobilized in fundoplication.
Protrusion of abdominal contents into the chest through a diaphragm rupture after blunt or penetrating trauma, more often on the left.
An enzyme that adds random nucleotides at V(D)J junctions, increasing antibody and T cell receptor diversity. A marker of lymphoblasts in ALL.
Long-lived B cells formed after antigen exposure that mount faster, higher-affinity responses on re-exposure.
A state where lymphocytes that encounter antigen without costimulation become unresponsive, a form of peripheral tolerance.
An MHC class II molecule presenting antigens to CD4 T cells.
An MHC class II molecule; HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 are associated with celiac disease and type 1 diabetes.
An inherited defect of immune function causing recurrent or unusual infections, such as SCID, Bruton agammaglobulinemia and DiGeorge syndrome.
Dimeric IgA joined by a J chain and secretory piece, found in mucosal secretions and breast milk, protecting mucosal surfaces.
An mTOR inhibitor used as an immunosuppressant for transplants and in some cancers and tuberous sclerosis.
Human leukocyte antigens: cell-surface proteins encoded by the MHC genes that present peptides to T cells and determine transplant compatibility.
Abnormal bone formation within muscle, often after trauma. The progressive form (fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva) is caused by ACVR1 mutation.
Several ribosomes translating a single mRNA at the same time, forming a bead-like cluster.
Inflammatory programmed cell death mediated by caspase-1 and gasdermin, with release of IL-1 beta.
Membrane-bound fragments of a dying cell formed during apoptosis, which are taken up by phagocytes.
Receptors for tumor necrosis factor. TNFR1 triggers inflammation or apoptosis through death domains.
Inherited failure of lymphocyte apoptosis (FAS pathway) causing lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and autoimmune cytopenias.
An industrial solvent that causes liver injury through free radicals, causing centrilobular necrosis and fatty change.
Inflammation of tissues around a joint, such as the shoulder (adhesive capsulitis).
A prostaglandin from mast cells that causes bronchoconstriction and vasodilation; mediates niacin flushing.
The first step in extravasation, when selectins on endothelium weakly bind white cells and slow them. Followed by integrin-mediated adhesion and transmigration.
Integrin alpha4beta1 on lymphocytes that binds VCAM-1 for migration into tissues. Blocked by natalizumab.
A colored product formed when tetrazolium dyes are reduced, used in the NBT test for neutrophil oxidative burst.
The protein mutated in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome that regulates actin cytoskeleton in blood cells.
The receptor mediating bradykinin's vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. Bradykinin buildup causes ACE inhibitor cough and angioedema.
A test of total complement activity of the classical pathway. Low in deficiencies of C1 through C9.
Receptors for complement fragments on phagocytes and B cells, such as CR1 and CR3, aiding opsonization.
Old term for IgE antibody that mediates immediate allergic reactions. Also refers to nonspecific antibodies detected in syphilis tests.
Calcium deposits in the skin, as in dermatomyositis, scleroderma and CREST syndrome.
Structural changes in vessel walls in response to injury or pressure, such as intimal thickening and wall hypertrophy in hypertension.
A tyrosine kinase receptor for fibroblast growth factors. Mutations cause skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia.
A receptor negatively regulating bone growth. Activating mutation causes achondroplasia.
A congenital chest wall deformity with a caved-in sternum.
Spongy bone formed by a lattice of trabeculae with marrow spaces, found in vertebrae and long bone ends. It is lost first in osteoporosis.
A joint between wrist bones and the metacarpals. The first (thumb) one is a saddle joint commonly affected by osteoarthritis.
An MHC class II allele; related alleles such as HLA-DR4 are associated with rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly and neutropenia.
An enzyme that splits pyrophosphate into two phosphates, driving reactions like DNA synthesis forward.
Inherited deficiency of alkaline phosphatase causing defective bone mineralization with low serum alkaline phosphatase and rickets-like bones.
Enzyme that attaches histidine to its tRNA. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies target it in dermatomyositis and polymyositis.
Regional muscle pain from trigger points, tight bands within muscle that are tender and refer pain.
A protein complex linking dystrophin inside muscle cells to the extracellular matrix.
The DMPK gene product. A CTG repeat expansion in DMPK causes myotonic dystrophy.
The depolarization of the muscle membrane at the neuromuscular junction when acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors, triggering a muscle action potential.
A transmembrane protein of tight junctions that seals the gaps between epithelial cells.
A desmosome protein linking intermediate filaments to the cell membrane. Mutated in some cardiomyopathies and skin disorders.
Proteins forming gap junction channels that allow direct passage of ions and small molecules between cells.
A plant-derived photosensitizing compound that, activated by UVA, treats psoriasis and vitiligo (PUVA).
A basement membrane collagen whose fragment, endostatin, inhibits blood vessel growth.
A rapidly growing, dome-shaped skin tumor with a central keratin plug, regarded as a low-grade squamous cell carcinoma that may regress.
A mole whose melanocyte nests lie entirely within the dermis, usually raised and flesh-colored.
Bulbous thickening of the nose from severe rosacea with sebaceous gland hyperplasia.
Inflammation of subcutaneous fat. Erythema nodosum is the common type, with tender red shin nodules.
A benign malformation of lymphatic vessels, including cystic hygroma in the neck in Turner syndrome.
A collection of lymph in a cavity, usually after surgery that disrupts lymphatics, such as pelvic lymph node dissection.
A group of skeletal disorders with stippled calcifications in cartilage and epiphyses. One form results from warfarin exposure in pregnancy.
An anticoagulant from leech saliva that directly inhibits thrombin. Recombinant forms (lepirudin, bivalirudin) are used.
An inducible COX enzyme that makes inflammatory prostaglandins. Selectively blocked by celecoxib.
Antiplatelet drugs that block the platelet ADP receptor, such as clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor.
A nonselective NSAID that inhibits COX enzymes, used for pain and arthritis. Adverse effects include GI ulcers and kidney injury.
An NSAID with preferential COX-2 inhibition, used for arthritis.
A long half-life NSAID used for arthritis.
The lowest antibiotic concentration that prevents visible bacterial growth in culture, used to judge susceptibility.
Fusion of adjacent fingers or toes, from failed apoptosis of interdigital webbing during limb development.
The upper layer of the bilaminar embryonic disc that forms the three germ layers during gastrulation. The hypoblast is the lower layer.
Early embryonic outgrowths of mesenchyme covered by ectoderm that develop into limbs. Thalidomide exposure disrupts them.
Cells at the edge of tooth pulp that make dentin.
Flattening or asymmetry of the skull, from positioning or premature suture fusion.
Fusion of the lower limbs, a mermaid-like malformation, with renal agenesis, associated with maternal diabetes.
Nerve network from C1 to C4 supplying neck muscles and skin, giving rise to the phrenic nerve (C3-5).
Backward displacement of the tongue base that can obstruct the airway, seen in Pierre Robin sequence.
Micrognathia leading to glossoptosis and a U-shaped cleft palate, causing airway obstruction and feeding difficulty.
Embryonic structure from the fourth pharyngeal pouch that forms the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid.
An extended-spectrum penicillin active against Pseudomonas, now rarely used.
Cephalosporins such as cefazolin and cephalexin, with good gram-positive and limited gram-negative activity, used for skin infections and surgical prophylaxis.
Beta-lactams related to cephalosporins, such as cefoxitin and cefotetan, with anaerobic activity and beta-lactamase stability.
Cephalosporins such as cefuroxime, cefoxitin and cefaclor with more gram-negative activity, including H. influenzae, than the first generation.
A bacterial protein subunit that lets RNA polymerase recognize promoters and start transcription.
A potent synthetic oral estrogen, the estrogen in most combined oral contraceptives.
A synthetic estrogen prodrug converted to ethinyl estradiol, used in oral contraceptives.
An oral synthetic anabolic steroid with little androgenic effect, used for weight gain and burns.
Drugs such as flutamide and bicalutamide that block androgen receptors, used for prostate cancer.
An intracellular protein that binds cyclosporine; the complex inhibits calcineurin and blocks T cell activation.
A cytokine that stimulates platelet production; recombinant oprelvekin was used for thrombocytopenia.
A monoclonal antibody against the p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23, used for psoriasis and Crohn disease.
A cytokine from dendritic cells that sustains Th17 cells; important in psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease.
Antibodies against antigens from another individual of the same species, such as anti-Rh or anti-HLA antibodies.
An enzyme removing phosphate from nucleotide 5' ends, raised in cholestasis; helps confirm that raised alkaline phosphatase is of liver origin.
Inherited failure of red cell production, as in Diamond-Blackfan anemia, with macrocytic anemia, low reticulocytes and congenital anomalies like thumb abnormalities.
A genus of gram-negative rods of the Enterobacteriaceae, a cause of urinary infections; produces urease like Proteus.
Toxicity from mercury: elemental vapor causes neurologic and psychiatric symptoms and tremor; organic mercury causes neurotoxicity; inorganic salts injure the kidney.
The continuation of the subclavian artery from the first rib to the teres major, supplying the shoulder. It is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor.
A break of the upper surface of the tibia at the knee, often from high-energy impact or a lateral blow (bumper fracture). Risks include compartment syndrome and knee instability.

Small-vessel vasculitis with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, including granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA), microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (p-ANCA).
An iodinated, high-osmolar radiographic contrast agent.
An iodinated contrast agent once used for oral cholecystography; it also reduces conversion of T4 to T3.
The slime of polysaccharides, proteins and DNA that bacteria secrete to adhere to surfaces and protect themselves from antibiotics and host defenses.
A tumor of the thymus in the anterior mediastinum, most often a thymoma associated with myasthenia gravis.
Inflammatory response to material that cannot be removed, with macrophages and giant cells forming granulomas around it.
Increased sensitivity to touch or sensory stimuli.
Elimination of self-reactive lymphocytes in primary lymphoid organs: T cells in the thymus (negative selection) and B cells in bone marrow.
A rare disease of smooth muscle cell growth in the lungs forming cysts, in women, associated with tuberous sclerosis. Causes dyspnea and pneumothorax.
Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1, a kinase promoting cell growth and protein synthesis. Blocked by sirolimus and everolimus.
Painful blue-purple toes with intact pulses from cholesterol or other emboli, often after vascular procedures or anticoagulation.
A double-membrane vesicle that engulfs cell components and fuses with lysosomes in autophagy. Its precursor is the phagophore.
Episode of severe pain in sickle cell disease when sickled red cells block small vessels, causing ischemia. Triggered by infection, dehydration or hypoxia.
The globin chain of fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2gamma2). Hydroxyurea raises gamma-globin expression in sickle cell disease.
A mold genus that produces penicillin; some species cause opportunistic infection, such as Talaromyces marneffei in AIDS.
Receptor for IL-13, found on epithelial and immune cells, which drives allergic inflammation. Dupilumab blocks IL-4/IL-13 signaling.
